## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no results yet, and scores stay hidden for the whole search. The only feedback will be whether each trial runs or fails. The final pick uses each trial's real 2-seed score, so the search works like a portfolio: each candidate should be a strong guess on its own, and the set should cover different ideas. The defaults give only about 32 PPO updates, so a cheaper recipe that collects more samples may help. On the network side, the agent must find where a brick will land (the highest column under its footprint) and then check the target at that exact layer. It also needs to know whether any missing target cells below would get sealed under the brick. The starting network mixes all layers in its first layer, so it has to learn that per-layer lookup indirectly. This round covers three things: the same network with a different recipe, a network that works layer by layer and softly picks the landing layer, and a starting network with more spatial context and global context.

### Round 2
Scores are hidden, so the only evidence is that all three Round 1 trials trained without errors and passed the checks. Ranking them is impossible. Looking at the task itself: a placement is correct when every cell under the footprint next needs a block at the same layer, and that layer equals the highest build column under the footprint. This rule is local, and the starting network's max/min/avg footprint pooling can in principle represent it. That points to sample efficiency and the update count as the likely bottleneck, since the default recipe gives only 32 updates. Ordering under overhangs and choosing DONE may also need wider context. So this round makes three different bets. The first changes the recipe only: one PPO epoch, which gives about 3.25 times the samples. The second gives the column features more depth and makes the footprint head two layers deep with global context. The third adds global self-attention after the convolutions.

### Round 3
Scores are hidden and all 6 trials trained without errors, so the evidence can't rank anything. What we have: every design and recipe ran within the time limit, including 1-epoch PPO at 405k steps (r2c1), so long cheap runs are safe. Because the final pick uses real 2-seed dev scores, the best use of the remaining trials is several plausible strong candidates. Refinements: (1) combine the r2c2 network (deeper column MLP, footprint heads that see global context) with the 1-epoch recipe, so it trains on about 349k fresh steps; (2) change only gamma and gae_lambda from r2c1, because the +1 exact-build bonus comes at episode end and gamma 0.95 discounts it heavily. New idea: (3) a deeper trunk with a dilated residual convolution for a wider view, plus footprint heads that see global context. Placing bricks under overhangs in the right order needs context beyond 5x5. It also uses the 1-epoch recipe.

### Round 4
Scores are hidden, so all I know is that every trial ran. The 1-epoch recipe (r2c1) gave 3x the default's environment steps and stayed inside the time limit, and so did networks up to 1.89x the starting compute. On this task the main thing should be how fast fresh designs are seen and how precisely each footprint's landing height is read. Neither seed noise nor scores can be judged from what I have. This last round should combine plausible pieces, not open new axes. (1) The richest network so far (dilated trunk with context heads) with a longer-horizon recipe, so the final +1 bonus gets more credit. (2) The deep-column network with the same longer horizon. (3) A new head idea: a learned convolution the size of each footprint over projected features. It sees each cell under the brick separately, not just the max, min and mean.
